## Antikythera shipwreck artifacts

The page does not provide museum inventory or catalog numbers for the shipwreck artifacts. It identifies the holding institution as the National Archaeological Museum in Athens for the recovered items generally and for the Antikythera mechanism specifically.

| Bronze statues | Bronze | Recovered during the first expedition in 1900–1901; the mechanism itself was retrieved in 1901 | Not stated | National Museum of Archaeology, Athens |
| Marble statues | Marble | Recovered during the first expedition in 1900–1901 | Not stated | National Museum of Archaeology, Athens |

### Artifact discoveries and expedition dates

- **Early 1900:** Captain Dimitrios Kontos and sponge divers from Symi discovered the Antikythera wreck.
- **1900–1901:** The first expedition with the Hellenic Royal Navy recovered:
  - Bronze statues
  - Marble statues
  - Pottery
  - Unique glassware
  - Jewellery
  - Coins
  - The Antikythera mechanism
- **1901, probably July:** The Antikythera mechanism was retrieved from the wreckage.
- **2012 and 2015:** Two further searches at the Antikythera wreck site yielded:
  - Art objects
  - A second ship that may be connected with the treasure ship on which the mechanism was found
  - A bronze disc embellished with the image of a bull
- The page states that the bronze disc was initially thought possibly to be part of the Antikythera mechanism, as a cog wheel, but that there is little evidence for this and it is more likely to have been a bronze decoration on a piece of furniture.
- **2014 and 2015:** Further dives were undertaken in the hope of discovering more of the mechanism.
- **2014–October 2019:** A five-year programme of investigations took place.
- **May 2020:** A new five-year investigation session began.

## Antikythera mechanism fragments

The page states that the mechanism was found as one lump, later separated into **three main fragments**, and that conservation efforts resulted in **82 separate fragments**. Of these, **seven are mechanically significant** and contain most of the mechanism and inscriptions. Another **16 smaller parts** contain fractional and incomplete inscriptions.

No museum inventory/catalog number is provided for the mechanism or any fragment.

| Fragment designation | Size | Weight | Gears | Inscriptions | Discovery/finding details and stated contents |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| **Fragment A** | **180 × 150 mm** | **369.1 g** | **27** | Yes | Main fragment containing the majority of the known mechanism. Contains the large **b1** gear; parts of the **l, m, c, and d** trains; the crank mechanism socket; the side-mounted gear meshing with **b1**; the rearmost **e** and **k** gears; the pin-and-slot mechanism of the **k** train; divisions of the upper-left quarter of the Saros spiral; **14 inscriptions** from that spiral; inscriptions for the exeligmos dial; remnants of the dial face on the back surface; and back-door inscriptions. Approximately **30 mm** thick at its thickest point. |
| **Fragment B** | **125 × 60 mm** | **99.4 g** | **1** | Yes | Contains approximately the bottom-right third of the Metonic spiral and inscriptions from both the spiral and the back door. The Metonic scale consisted of **235 cells**, of which **49** have been deciphered from Fragment B either wholly or partially. Contains the **o1** gear used in the Olympic train. |
| **Fragment C** | **120 × 110 mm** | **63.8 g** | **1** | Yes | Contains parts of the upper-right front dial face showing calendar and zodiac inscriptions. Contains the Moon indicator dial assembly, including the Moon-phase sphere in its housing, and the **ma1** bevel gear used in the Moon-phase indication system. |
| **Fragment D** | **45 × 35 mm** | **15.0 g** | **1** | Not stated | Contains at least one unknown gear. Michael T. Wright considered that it possibly contains two; Xenophon Moussas considered it to contain one gear numbered **45 “ME”** inside a hollow gear, giving the position of Jupiter through epicyclic motion. |
| **Fragment E** | **60 × 35 mm** | **22.1 g** | Not stated | Yes | **Found in 1976.** Contains **six inscriptions** from the upper-right of the Saros spiral. |
| **Fragment F** | **90 × 80 mm** | **86.2 g** | Not stated | Yes | **Found in 2005.** Contains **16 inscriptions** from the lower-right of the Saros spiral and remnants of the mechanism’s wooden housing. |
| **Fragment G** | **125 × 110 mm** | **31.7 g** | Not stated | Yes | A combination of fragments taken from Fragment C while cleaning. |

### Other numbered or designated mechanism fragments and parts

- **Fragment 19**
  - Contains significant back-door inscriptions.
  - One inscription reads **“… 76 years …”**, referring to the Callippic cycle.
  - Other inscriptions appear to describe the function of the back dials.
- **Fragment E**
  - Contains the wording **“on the spiral subdivisions 235”**, referring to the Metonic dial.
- **Fragment F**
  - Contains remnants of the wooden housing.
- **Fragment D**
  - Includes the gear designation **45 “ME”** according to Xenophon Moussas.
- The page states that **15 further minor fragments** have remnants of inscriptions, in addition to Fragment 19.
- The page does not give individual designations or numbers for those 15 minor fragments.
- The page states that other fragments may still be in storage and undiscovered since their initial recovery.

### Antikythera Mechanism fragment designations and numbers

- Fragment designations: Not stated.
- Fragment numbers: Not stated.
- The page states that the remaining fragments contain **30 gears** in a highly complex arrangement.
- The device was originally housed in a wooden-framed case measuring **31.5 × 19 × 10 cm**.
- The case had front and back doors, with astronomical inscriptions covering much of the exterior.
- Construction date: **150–100 BC**.
- Discovery year: **1901**.

### 2014 expedition artifacts and dates

The first season of the “Return to Antikythera” project took place from **September 15 to October 7, 2014**. The following objects or components were recovered:

- Multiple lead anchors, over **1 meter long**.
- A bronze rigging ring with fragments of wood still attached.
- Hull planks.
- A beautiful intact table jug.
- Part of an ornate bed leg.
- A **2-meter-long bronze spear**, buried just beneath the surface of the sand.

The page does not provide museum inventory/catalog numbers, fragment designations, fragment numbers, or holding institutions for these objects.
